Case Vignette: Mrs. A.

Mrs. A. is an 80-year-old West African woman, married for fifty-seven years to her husband, a retired schoolteacher. She has been a pastor for over forty years, leading a small but devoted congregation in a mid-sized American city. She came to therapy at the urging of her adult daughter, who noticed that her mother had stopped leaving the house except for Sunday services, and even then, she often cut the sermon short.

The trauma began in 1994, during the Rwandan genocide. Mrs. A. and her family lived in a rural village near the border. She was a midwife and lay preacher at the time. One afternoon, armed men came to her compound. They were neighbors, men she had baptized. They demanded to know where her husband was hiding. She lied, saying he had fled to the capital. They did not believe her. They forced her to kneel in the dirt courtyard while they ransacked her home. She remembers the sun on her neck, the smell of burning from a nearby house, and the sound of a rooster crowing—a sound that now makes her chest tighten. They did not kill her, but they killed her younger brother, who had been hiding in the latrine. She found his body that evening. She and her husband fled that night, walking for three days to the border. She carried her youngest child, then two years old, on her back. She did not sleep for four days.

In the refugee camp, she resumed preaching. She held services under a tarp, using a plastic bucket as a pulpit. She told her congregation, “We will not be broken.” But inside, she felt hollow. She had nightmares of the red dirt turning to blood. She avoided thinking about her brother’s face. She told herself God had spared her for a reason.

Now, thirty years later, she is in the United States. She became a pastor here, first in a storefront church, then in a proper building. For decades, she managed. She prayed over her congregation, counseled the grieving, baptized the young. But the symptoms have worsened with age. She has trouble sleeping. She wakes at 3:00 AM, convinced she hears machetes scraping against the sidewalk. She has stopped watching the news, because any image of conflict—even a traffic dispute—sends her heart racing. She avoids large crowds, especially if they are loud. She no longer attends community events, which she once loved. She tells herself it is because she is old and tired.

Her husband has become her primary support. He makes sure she eats, drives her to church, and holds her hand during thunderstorms. She has not told him about the full extent of her nightmares. She fears burdening him.

At her last sermon, she spoke for only twelve minutes. Her hands trembled on the Bible. She forgot the passage she was reading. She looked at the faces in the pews—mostly African immigrants, some who had also fled war—and she felt a sudden, overwhelming urge to run. She excused herself to the vestry and sat alone for twenty minutes, breathing shallowly, her palms sweating. She has not told anyone in the congregation.

She came to therapy reluctantly. She said, “I am supposed to be the one who helps others. I am supposed to have faith.” She sat upright in the chair, her posture rigid, her hands folded in her lap. She looked at the floor when she spoke about the genocide. She said, “I have prayed for God to take these memories from me. But they stay. They stay like a stone in my chest.”

She continues to attend church every Sunday. She continues to pray. But she no longer feels the presence of God in the same way. She feels, instead, a quiet distance, as if she is speaking to a wall. She does not know how to reconcile her faith with the fact that the men who killed her brother were men she had blessed. She does not know how to reconcile her calling with the fact that she now fears her own congregation.
